- [2023/05/21] Figure 4 provides an overview of SAV deployment statistics for packets both outbound from and inbound to measured networks as of August 1, 2019.
- [2023/05/21] The data is presented by IPv4/24 prefixes and IPv6/40 prefixes, and by autonomous systems (ASes).
- [2023/05/21] According to the findings, while most networks block packets with spoofed source IP addresses, deployment of SAV is far from universal.
- [2023/05/21] 25.2% and 32.1% of tested IPv4 and IPv6 ASes respectively had at least one prefix where operators did not deploy SAV to block outbound spoofed packets to the Internet.
- [2023/05/21] Inbound filtering of spoofed packets is less deployed than outbound filtering, despite these packets being a threat to receiving networks.
- [2023/05/21] For IPv4 tests received in May 2006 and the year ending August 2019, 18.3% and 14.9% of IPv4/24 prefixes respectively did not block spoofed-source packets from leaving their networks.
- [2023/05/21] The deployment of SAV has not generally improved between May 2006 and the year ending August 2019.
- [2023/05/21] Figure 5 shows no correlation between prefix age (measured as first appearance in global BGP routing table) and probability of SAV deployment.
- [2023/05/21] The authors attempted to mitigate sampling concerns by daemonizing the Spoofer client, which allows for automatic gathering of longitudinal data.
- [2023/05/21] Even with the daemonized client, 44% of IPv4 /24 prefixes and 32% of ASes reported measurements in only a single week between May 2016 and August 2019.
- [2023/05/21] The model's predictive recall has increased significantly from around 20% in May 2016 to over 80% for IPv6 by August 2019, but only 50-70% for IPv4.
- [2023/05/21] NAT systems are not a substitute for SAV; 6.4% of IPv4 /24 prefixes tested from clients behind a NAT did not filter packets with spoofed source addresses in the year ending August 2019.
- [2023/05/21] In practice, there are two failure modes where a NAT will forward packets with spoofed source addresses: it either forwards them intact or rewrites the source address to its publicly routable address.
